name: Disposable respirators (N95, FFP2, FFP3, P100)
summary: Disposable masks of filter material that, when NIOSH-approved and sealed to a clean-shaven face, filter out fine dust, mould spores, smoke particles and airborne germs.
uses: Mould, fibreglass, plaster, sawdust and other fine dust: N95, FFP2 or better. Lead dust: P100 or FFP3, sealed to a shaven face
Asbestos: don't rely on one. OSHA bans filtering masks for asbestos work; HSE accepts FFP3 only for short non-licensed jobs. Use a half mask with P100 or P3 filters
Wildfire smoke and ash particles, but not the gases in smoke
Airborne germs such as TB when it fits; a plain N95 is not splash protection (only 'surgical N95' types have a splash-resistant outer layer)
No use against gas, vapour or carbon monoxide, and none where oxygen is low: silos, tanks, pits and other confined spaces
Works only if it seals: beard or stubble under the edge lets dust straight in, and a seal check is not a fit test
identify: A cup, fold-flat or duckbill mask of filter fabric with two head straps, a nose clip and sometimes an outlet valve. US classes: N (not oil-resistant), R (somewhat oil-resistant), P (strongly oil-resistant), each at 95, 99 or 100, where 100 means 99.97% (NIOSH FFR page). An approved one must have printed on it the maker's or private-label name, NIOSH or its logo, a TC-84A-xxxx number, the class (N95, P100 and so on) and a model or part number; missing any, it is not approved (NIOSH label sheet; NIOSH N95 check). Fake signs: marks missing, NIOSH misspelt, sequins or fabric decoration, claims to fit children, ear loops with no clip joining them behind the head; a real number can be copied onto a fake (NIOSH counterfeit FFRs). Europe: EN 149 with FFP1, FFP2 or FFP3, then NR (one shift) or R (reusable), and D if it passed the clogging test (Centexbel FFP); HSE rates them 4, 10 and 20 (HSE HSG53). Canada accepts NIOSH-approved masks and CSA-certified ones marked CA-N95, CA-N99 or CA-N100 under CSA Z94.4.1; older Health Canada 95PFE masks are also listed (CCOHS healthcare; Health Canada CSA notice). Australia and NZ: P1, P2, P3 (UWA respiratory protection). KN95s are not NIOSH-approved (NIOSH misrepresented masks). CDC says about 60% of KN95 respirators NIOSH evaluated in 2020 and 2021 did not meet the requirements they intended to meet (CDC mask types). In NIOSH's tests of respirators claiming international standards, most of them claiming the Chinese KN95 standard, 35% of 356 tests found every unit under 95% filtration and 26% found some units over and some under (NIOSH KN95 tests). NIOSH adds that ear loops may limit a tight fit (NIOSH KN95 tests).
test: A found one should be dry and clean, not crushed or creased through the filter, with both straps soft, not hard or stiff, and firmly attached (in a NIOSH stockpile study nine hardened straps on one 12-year-old model broke when put on, NIOSH stockpile fit) and the nose clip and foam intact; throw it out if it smells, shows mould or is damaged (NIOSH shelf life). Past its printed date it no longer counts as approved, but NIOSH found 98% of stockpiled respirators aged 5 to 12 years still met its performance tests (NIOSH shelf life); fit after long storage varied by product and lot (NIOSH stockpile fit). To put it on: top strap high on the back of the head, bottom strap round the neck below the ears, straps not crossed, then mould the nose clip with the fingertips of both hands (NIOSH donning guide). Seal check every time: cover it with both hands and take a quick breath in, then breathe out. Air at the nose means reshape the clip; at the edges, adjust the straps; if it still leaks, try another size or model (NIOSH donning guide). Facial hair under the edge stops it sealing (OSHA 1910.134; CDC fit testing). A seal check is not a fit test (NIOSH FFR page); at work OSHA requires a fit test before first use and every year, for each respirator model (CDC fit testing). Replace it when it is damaged, soiled, wet or harder to breathe through (NIOSH shelf life; NIOSH FFR page; EPA smoke factsheet). After asbestos work, bin it as asbestos waste after one use (HSE EM6).

decay.note: Estimate. Many disposables carry a five-year shelf life, past which NIOSH no longer counts them approved (NIOSH shelf life). Old stock mostly still filtered, but fit varied and hardened straps broke on one 12-year-old model (NIOSH stockpile fit). Heat, sun, damp and dust shorten life.

improvise: Better: a half or full mask with P100 filters (magenta, NIOSH 42 CFR 84.179) or P3. Asbestos: OSHA bars filtering facepieces and asks for at least a half mask with HEPA filters, more for heavy jobs (OSHA asbestos); HSE accepts a disposable FFP3 only for short non-licensed work, never over stubble (HSE EM6). Lead needs N100, R100 or P100 filters (OSHA lead). Mould: at least an N95, and a half or full mask for long tear-outs (CDC mold cleanup); fibreglass dust: any N95-class filter (NIOSH fibrous glass). Surgical masks, cloth and bandanas, wet or dry, don't seal and stop little of the finest dust (NIOSH wildfire smoke). Ear-loop KN95s aren't NIOSH-approved and may not seal (NIOSH KN95 tests; EPA smoke factsheet); approved ear-loop designs join the loops behind the head (NIOSH N95 check). If that's all you have, seal-check it: any leak means no seal (NIOSH donning guide). A replaced strap voids the approval, and a seal check isn't a fit test (NIOSH N95 check; NIOSH FFR page), so don't count on a repaired one for lead or asbestos. Beards: shave where the edge seals; only loose hooded powered respirators work with beards (CDC fit testing). Never against carbon monoxide, gas, vapour or the gases in smoke, or where oxygen is low, as in silos, tanks and pits: it filters particles and adds no oxygen (NIOSH FFR page; HSE HSG53; Alberta producers).
